## Summary
We looked at whether students’ family backgrounds and study habits could help predict who attended paid mathematics classes. Using data from 395 students at two Portuguese schools, we compared three models. Logistic regression performed best during cross-validation, with an average accuracy of 64.2%. On the test data, its accuracy was 58.6%, slightly higher than the 54.5% accuracy of always predicting the most common outcome. This suggests the information in our dataset offers some help with prediction, but the results are modest. The data covers only two schools, and the model doesn’t include every possible reason a student might attend tutoring. It also shows patterns in the data, not that a student’s background or study habits cause them to take paid classes.

## Introduction

Private tutoring provides students with additional academic instruction outside regular school lessons. This includes help with coursework and examination preparation. In their study of tutoring agencies in Ontario, Aurini and Davies (2004) describe how private tutoring expanded from informal assistance into organized learning centres that offer a broader range of educational services. This suggests that paid tuition is becoming a trend. However, we believe that participation in paid tutoring may reflect more than academic difficulty. Using German household survey data, Hille, Spieß, and Staneva (2016) document differences in tutoring participation across income groups. They highlighted the importance of considering family resources when studying access to supplementary education. In Portugal, Fonseca (1996) examines how family resources and competition for educational qualifications shape educational opportunities and strategies. Although this research concerns higher education rather than mathematics tutoring specifically, it still provides historical context for examining family background in educational participation. More directly, Qu (2025) analyzes mathematics achievement among students in two Portuguese secondary schools. This research considered family, individual, and school-related characteristics, including paid tutoring. Building on these perspectives, our study aim to understand which student characteristics help distinguish participants from non-participants. This may inform further research into access to supplementary learning opportunities. We ask: Can students’ family backgrounds and study-related characteristics predict whether they attend paid tutoring in mathematics? To answer this question, we use the mathematics subset of the Student Performance dataset from the UCI Machine Learning Repository (Cortez 2008). It contains 395 student records from two Portuguese secondary schools, collected through school reports and questionnaires. Where each row represents one student’s record for the mathematics course. Our predictors include parental education and occupations, family size, parents’ cohabitation status, guardian, weekly study time, previous class failures, and family and school educational support. The response variable is paid mathematics tutoring participation, recorded as “yes” or “no”. Which makes this a binary classification problem. We exclude first-period, second-period, and final grades because these may already reflect tutoring participation. Our analysis evaluates predictive relationships within this sample. It does not establish why students attend tutoring or whether tutoring improves their grades.

## Methods

### Data
```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
```

```{r}
url <- "https://archive.ics.uci.edu/static/public/320/student+performance.zip"

download.file(url,"../data/raw/student_performance.zip", mode = "wb")
unzip("../data/raw/student_performance.zip", exdir = "../data/raw")
unzip("../data/raw/student.zip", exdir = "../data/raw")
student_math <- read_delim("../data/raw/student-mat.csv", delim = ";")

file.remove("../data/raw/student_performance.zip", "../data/raw/student.zip")
```

```{r}
student_math_clean <- student_math |> 
  select(paid, Medu, Fedu, Mjob, Fjob, famsize, Pstatus, studytime, 
         failures, famsup, school, address) |> 
  rename(paid_classes = paid,
         mother_edu = Medu,
         father_edu = Fedu,
         mother_job = Mjob,
         father_job = Fjob,
         family_size = famsize, 
         parent_status = Pstatus, 
         past_failures = failures,
         family_support = famsup
         ) |> 
  mutate(address = case_when(address == "U" ~ "urban", 
                             address == "R" ~ "rural"),
         parent_status = case_when(parent_status == "T" ~ "together",
                                   parent_status == "A" ~ "apart"),
         family_size = case_when(family_size == "LE3" ~ "3 or fewer", 
                                 family_size == "GT3" ~ "greater than 3"),
         school = case_when(school == "GP" ~ "Gabriel Pereira",
                            school == "MS" ~ "Mousinho da Silveira")) |> 
  mutate(across(where(is.character), as.factor)) |> 
  mutate(studytime = factor(studytime, levels = 1:4,
                            labels = c("<2 hours", "2-5 hours", 
                                       "5-10 hours", ">10 hours")),
         paid_classes = factor(paid_classes, levels = c("yes", "no")))
  

write_csv(student_math_clean, "../data/processed/student_math_clean.csv")

head(student_math_clean)
```

### Analysis
```{r}
#| include: false
library(reticulate)
use_virtualenv("../.venv", required = TRUE)
```

```{python}
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
```

```{python}
math_student = pd.read_csv("../data/processed/student_math_clean.csv")

# Splitting the data into 75% training and 25% test
train_df, test_df = train_test_split(math_student, test_size = 0.25, stratify=math_student["paid_classes"], random_state = 522)

train_df.to_csv("../data/processed/student_math_train.csv", index=False)
test_df.to_csv("../data/processed/student_math_test.csv", index=False)

print(train_df.shape, test_df.shape)
print(train_df["paid_classes"].value_counts())
```

### Classification Model

We compare three classifiers using five-fold stratified cross-validation on the training data. The model with the highest mean validation accuracy is selected. We then fit that model on the full training set and report its performance once on the held-out test set. The test set is not used to choose a model.

We use logistic regression as a simple linear baseline, a shallow decision tree for an interpretable rule-based model, and a small random forest to check whether combining trees improves prediction. The categorical predictors are one-hot encoded, and numeric predictors are standardized within each training fold. The same preprocessing is applied consistently to all three models.

#### Cross-validation model comparison

```{python}
#| echo: true

import numpy as np
import altair as alt
from IPython.display import display
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold, cross_val_score
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, precision_score, recall_score, f1_score, confusion_matrix

# These are the selected predictors; the response is paid_classes.
categorical_columns = [
    "mother_job", "father_job", "family_size", "parent_status",
    "studytime", "family_support", "school", "address"
]
numeric_columns = ["mother_edu", "father_edu", "past_failures"]
predictor_columns = categorical_columns + numeric_columns

X_train = train_df[predictor_columns]
y_train = train_df["paid_classes"].astype(str)
X_test = test_df[predictor_columns]
y_test = test_df["paid_classes"].astype(str)

preprocessor = ColumnTransformer(
    transformers=[
        ("numeric", StandardScaler(), numeric_columns),
        ("categorical", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), categorical_columns),
    ]
)

model_choices = {
    "Logistic regression": LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, random_state=522),
    "Decision tree (depth 4)": DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=4, random_state=522),
    "Random forest": RandomForestClassifier(
        n_estimators=100, max_depth=5, random_state=522, n_jobs=-1
    ),
}

cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=522)
model_pipelines = {}
cv_rows = []

for model_name, classifier in model_choices.items():
    pipeline = Pipeline([
        ("preprocess", preprocessor),
        ("classifier", classifier),
    ])
    scores = cross_val_score(
        pipeline, X_train, y_train, cv=cv, scoring="accuracy"
    )
    model_pipelines[model_name] = pipeline
    cv_rows.append({
        "Model": model_name,
        "Mean validation accuracy": scores.mean(),
        "SD across folds": scores.std(),
    })

cv_results = pd.DataFrame(cv_rows).sort_values(
    "Mean validation accuracy", ascending=False
).reset_index(drop=True)

print("Table 1. Five-fold cross-validation accuracy on training data.")
cv_results.style.format({
    "Mean validation accuracy": "{:.3f}",
    "SD across folds": "{:.3f}",
})

cv_chart = alt.Chart(cv_results).mark_bar().encode(
    x=alt.X("Model:N", sort="-y", title="Model"),
    y=alt.Y(
        "Mean validation accuracy:Q",
        scale=alt.Scale(domain=[0, 1]),
        title="Mean validation accuracy",
    ),
    tooltip=[
        alt.Tooltip("Model:N"),
        alt.Tooltip("Mean validation accuracy:Q", format=".3f"),
        alt.Tooltip("SD across folds:Q", format=".3f"),
    ],
).properties(width=450, height=280, title="Model accuracy across five validation folds")
cv_chart
```

**Figure 1.** Mean five-fold validation accuracy for each candidate model.

```{python}
#| echo: true
best_model_name = cv_results.loc[0, "Model"]
best_model = model_pipelines[best_model_name]
print(f"Selected model: {best_model_name}")
```

Logistic regression was selected because it had the highest mean validation accuracy across the five folds. We then used it to evaluate performance on the held-out test set.

## Results

### Exploratory Data Analysis

We used the training set to summarize the participation in paid mathematics classes. We want to examine whether participation varied by weekly study time. Table 1 reports the number and percentage of students in each participation group. Of the 296 students, 136 (45.9%) attended paid classes and 160 (54.1%) did not. Therefore the two groups are fairly balanced, with slightly more students in the non-participation group.

```{python}
paid_summary = (
       train_df["paid_classes"]
       .value_counts(dropna=False)
       .rename_axis("Attended paid classes")
       .reset_index(name="Students")
)

paid_summary["Percent"] = (
       100 * paid_summary["Students"] / len(train_df)
).round(1)

print(paid_summary.to_string(index=False))
```

The dataset records weekly study time in four categories: less than 2 hours, 2-5 hours, 5-10 hours and more than 10 hours. Figure 2 shows the percentage of students attending paid classes within each study-time group, using only the training set. Participation in paid mathematics classes was higher among students who reported more weekly study time. About 33% of students who studied less than 2 hours per week attended paid classes, and compare with about 62% of those who studied more than 10 hours per week. (Figure 2).

```{python}
import altair as alt

study_order = ["<2 hours", "2-5 hours", "5-10 hours", ">10 hours"]

# Calculate the proportion of students who attended paid classes in each study-time group.
study_summary = (
       train_df.dropna(subset=["studytime", "paid_classes"])
       .assign(attend=lambda df: df["paid_classes"].eq("yes"))
       .groupby("studytime", as_index=False)
       .agg(participation_rate=("attend", "mean"))
)

# Plot each group's participation rate as a percentage, ordered by weekly study time.
alt.Chart(study_summary).mark_bar().encode(
       y=alt.Y(
              "studytime:N",
              title="Weekly study time",
              sort=["<2 hours", "2-5 hours", "5-10 hours", ">10 hours"]
       ),
       x=alt.X(
              "participation_rate:Q",
              title="Percentage attending paid mathematics classes",
              axis=alt.Axis(format=".0%"),
              scale=alt.Scale(domain=[0,1]),
       ),
).properties(width=500, height=180)
```

**Figure 2.** Percentage of students attending paid mathematics classes within each weekly study-time group in the training set.

### Held-out test results

The selected model is refit using all training observations, then evaluated on the test observations that were set aside before cross-validation. We report accuracy and the precision, recall, and F1 score for students who attended paid mathematics classes. The majority-class baseline always predicts the most common outcome in the training data.

```{python}
#| echo: true

best_model.fit(X_train, y_train)
test_predictions = best_model.predict(X_test)
majority_class = y_train.mode().iloc[0]
baseline_predictions = np.repeat(majority_class, len(y_test))

results = pd.DataFrame([
    {
        "Model": best_model_name,
        "Accuracy": accuracy_score(y_test, test_predictions),
        "Precision (yes)": precision_score(
            y_test, test_predictions, pos_label="yes", zero_division=0
        ),
        "Recall (yes)": recall_score(
            y_test, test_predictions, pos_label="yes", zero_division=0
        ),
        "F1 (yes)": f1_score(
            y_test, test_predictions, pos_label="yes", zero_division=0
        ),
    },
    {
        "Model": "Majority-class baseline",
        "Accuracy": accuracy_score(y_test, baseline_predictions),
        "Precision (yes)": precision_score(
            y_test, baseline_predictions, pos_label="yes", zero_division=0
        ),
        "Recall (yes)": recall_score(
            y_test, baseline_predictions, pos_label="yes", zero_division=0
        ),
        "F1 (yes)": f1_score(
            y_test, baseline_predictions, pos_label="yes", zero_division=0
        ),
    },
])

print("Table 2. Held-out test metrics for the selected model and majority baseline.")
results.style.format({
    "Accuracy": "{:.3f}",
    "Precision (yes)": "{:.3f}",
    "Recall (yes)": "{:.3f}",
    "F1 (yes)": "{:.3f}",
})

cm = confusion_matrix(y_test, test_predictions, labels=["no", "yes"])
confusion = pd.DataFrame(
    cm,
    index=pd.Index(["no", "yes"], name="Actual"),
    columns=pd.Index(["no", "yes"], name="Predicted"),
)
print("Table 3. Confusion matrix for the selected model on the held-out test set.")
display(confusion)

cm_long = (
    confusion.rename_axis(index="Actual")
    .reset_index()
    .melt(id_vars="Actual", var_name="Predicted", value_name="Count")
)
heatmap = alt.Chart(cm_long).mark_rect().encode(
    x=alt.X("Predicted:N", sort=["no", "yes"], title="Predicted outcome"),
    y=alt.Y("Actual:N", sort=["no", "yes"], title="Actual outcome"),
    color=alt.Color("Count:Q", scale=alt.Scale(scheme="blues"), title="Students"),
    tooltip=["Actual:N", "Predicted:N", "Count:Q"],
).properties(width=300, height=260, title="Held-out test confusion matrix")
cell_text = heatmap.mark_text(fontSize=18).encode(text="Count:Q", color=alt.value("black"))
heatmap + cell_text
```

**Figure 3.** Confusion matrix for the selected model on the held-out test set.

The five-fold cross-validation comparison selected logistic regression, with a mean validation accuracy of 64.2% (standard deviation 2.4 percentage points). On the held-out test set, it achieved 58.6% accuracy, compared with 54.5% for the majority-class baseline. For students who attended paid classes, precision was 53.8%, recall was 62.2%, and F1 was 0.577. The confusion matrix shows 28 correctly identified students who attended classes, 30 correctly identified students who did not, 24 false positives, and 17 false negatives. Table 1 is used only for model selection; Tables 2 and 3 and Figure 2 report final test-set performance.

## Discussion

The results provide a limited answer to our research question. Logistic regression performed best in cross-validation, but its 58.6% test accuracy was only slightly higher than the 54.5% majority-class baseline. It correctly identified 28 of the 45 students who attended paid mathematics classes and 30 of the 54 who did not. However, it also predicted tutoring for 24 students who did not attend, and missed 17 who did. So, while the selected characteristics may help distinguish between the two groups, they do not give a reliable prediction for an individual student.

We expected family and study-related characteristics to provide some useful information, since decisions about extra classes may be connected to students’ learning experiences and family circumstances. But this dataset cannot tell us why a student attended tutoring, and our model does not include factors such as family income, academic goals, or a student’s perceived need for extra help. The data also cover only 395 students from two schools in Portugal, so the results may not apply to students in other schools or countries. Finally, these are associations used for prediction; they do not show that a particular background or study habit causes a student to attend paid classes.

A useful next step would be to repeat the analysis with students from more schools and include measures of tutoring access, family resources, and reasons for seeking extra help. That could help determine whether the modest performance here reflects limits in the predictors, the small sample, or both.
